title: Instant Pot Québec-Style Yellow Split Pea Soup with Ham
dek: Yellow split peas, smoky ham, carrots and savory herbs pressure-cook into a thick, comforting soup with no overnight soaking.
image_alt: Thick golden yellow split pea soup with shredded ham, diced carrots, black pepper and fresh herbs in a white bowl
ingredients: 1 tsp dried savory or dried thyme
1/2 tsp ground black pepper, plus more for serving
1 lb dried yellow split peas, sorted and rinsed well
1 1/4 lb meaty smoked ham hock or ham shank
1 1/2 cups diced fully cooked ham, about 8 oz
1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more only if needed

instructions.name: Soften the vegetables
instructions.text: Select Sauté on a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Add the oil, onion, carrots and celery; cook for 5 minutes, stirring often, until the onion softens. Add the garlic, savory, marjoram and pepper and cook for 30 seconds. Cancel Sauté.

instructions.name: Deglaze completely
instructions.text: Pour in 1 cup broth and scrape the base with a wooden spoon until no browned bits remain. This clean, thin-liquid layer helps prevent a burn warning.

instructions.name: Layer the soup
instructions.text: Add the remaining 5 cups broth and the water. Stir in the rinsed split peas and bay leaf, then nestle the ham hock into the liquid. Do not add the diced ham yet. The contents must stay below the half-full line because split peas expand and foam; do not double this recipe in a 6-quart pot.

instructions.name: Pressure cook and release naturally
instructions.text: Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 15 minutes. Allow about 15 minutes for the pot to pressurize, then let pressure release naturally for at least 15 minutes. If the valve is still raised, use a controlled release in short pulses only when the vent is quiet; stop immediately if foamy liquid sputters. Never force the lid, and wait for the float valve to drop.

instructions.name: Shred the ham
instructions.text: Open the lid away from your face. Transfer the ham hock to a board, discard the skin, bone and excess fat, and shred the meat. Remove the bay leaf. Stir the soup vigorously for 30 seconds to make it creamy while leaving visible peas and carrots.

instructions.name: Finish and season
instructions.text: Select Sauté. Return the shredded meat and add the diced cooked ham. Simmer for 3 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the ham is steaming hot and the soup reaches 165°F. Turn off the cooker, stir in the vinegar and taste before adding the salt. Ladle into bowls and finish with parsley and black pepper.

why_it_works: Yellow split peas break down under pressure without soaking, naturally thickening the soup while the diced vegetables remain recognizable.
Seven cups of thin liquid sit against a fully deglazed base, supplying dependable steam before the foamy legumes begin to expand.
A long natural release keeps starchy foam away from the valve, while vinegar added at the end brightens the smoky pork without slowing pea softening.
swaps: Replace the ham hock and diced ham with one smoked turkey leg; remove its skin and bones after cooking and verify the meat reaches 165°F.
For a meatless soup, omit both hams, use vegetable broth and add 1 teaspoon smoked paprika with the dried herbs; season more generously at the end.
Green split peas work with the same liquid and timing, though the color and earthy flavor will differ from Québec-style yellow pea soup.
storage: Cool in shallow containers within 2 hours and refrigerate for up to 4 days. The soup thickens substantially; reheat on the stove or with Sauté using 2 to 4 tablespoons water per portion, stirring until it reaches 165°F. Freeze airtight for up to 3 months and thaw overnight in the refrigerator.
notes: Use dried split peas, not whole dried peas or lentils; their pressure times and finished texture differ.
Ham and broth salinity varies, so add only the initial small amount of salt after pressure cooking and tasting.
Keep the base mild for the family and offer hot sauce or crushed red pepper at the table.
Written for a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Follow the minimum-liquid, fill-limit and release instructions in your exact model manual.
Beans and split peas can foam: stay below the half-full line and use the full natural release rather than an immediate quick release.

faqs.q: Do yellow split peas need to be soaked first?
faqs.a: No. Sort and rinse them well, then use them dry. Soaking changes the liquid balance and can make this pressure-cooker version thinner than intended.

faqs.q: Why is my pea soup too thick?
faqs.a: Split pea soup continues to thicken as it stands. Stir in warm water or unsalted broth 1/4 cup at a time until it is spoonable, then recheck seasoning.

faqs.q: Can I quick-release the pressure to save time?
faqs.a: Do not immediately quick-release split peas. Their starch can foam through the valve. Give the pot at least 15 minutes of natural release and use short controlled pulses only if the vent remains quiet and your model manual permits it.

title: Instant Pot Saffron Shrimp Risotto with Lemon & Chives
dek: Golden saffron rice turns creamy under pressure, then tender shrimp, lemon and chives finish the risotto without constant stirring.
image_alt: Creamy golden saffron risotto topped with curled shrimp, chopped chives and fine red saffron threads in a white bowl
ingredients: 4 cups low-sodium seafood stock or chicken broth, divided
1 1/4 lb large peeled and deveined shrimp, tails removed
1/2 cup dry white wine or additional broth
Extra saffron threads or mild chile threads, optional for serving

instructions.name: Bloom the saffron
instructions.text: Warm 1/2 cup of the broth until steaming, stir in the crushed saffron and set aside for 5 minutes. Pat the shrimp dry and season with 1/4 teaspoon salt; keep refrigerated while the rice cooks.

instructions.name: Toast the rice
instructions.text: Select Sauté on a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Add the oil and shallot and cook for 2 minutes. Add the garlic and Arborio rice and stir for 2 minutes, until the grains look chalky at the center and lightly toasted at the edges.

instructions.name: Deglaze and add thin liquid
instructions.text: Pour in the wine and scrape every browned bit from the base; simmer for 1 minute. Cancel Sauté. Add the saffron broth, remaining 3 1/2 cups broth and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. Stir once to distribute the rice, making sure it remains below the half-full line.

instructions.name: Pressure cook and release carefully
instructions.text: Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 5 minutes; allow about 10 minutes to reach pressure. Use a controlled quick release in short pulses, keeping hands and face away from the steam. Pause if starchy foam sputters, then continue only when the vent is quiet. Open after the float valve drops.

instructions.name: Cook the shrimp in the hot risotto
instructions.text: Stir the rice vigorously for 30 seconds. Select Sauté on Low, fold in the cold shrimp and cook for 3 to 5 minutes, stirring often, until every shrimp is opaque and reaches 145°F. If the risotto looks stiff, add hot broth or water 2 tablespoons at a time.

instructions.name: Finish off heat
instructions.text: Cancel Sauté. Stir in 2 tablespoons butter, Parmesan, lemon zest, 1 tablespoon lemon juice and half the chives. Cover loosely for 2 minutes, then adjust salt and lemon. Spoon into warm bowls, top with the remaining tablespoon butter and chives, and add a few saffron or mild chile threads if desired.

why_it_works: Unrinsed Arborio rice retains the surface starch that creates risotto's creamy body once the pressurized grains are stirred.
The shrimp go in only after pressure cooking, preventing the rubbery texture that a full rice cycle would cause.
Blooming saffron in warm broth distributes its aroma and golden color evenly instead of leaving concentrated bitter threads.
swaps: Use sea scallops cut into 1-inch pieces and cook them after pressure release just until opaque and 145°F.
For an alcohol-free version, replace the wine with broth and add an extra teaspoon of lemon juice at the end.
Pecorino Romano can replace Parmesan, but reduce the added salt because Pecorino is generally saltier.
storage: Cool leftovers within 2 hours and refrigerate airtight for up to 2 days. Reheat gently on the stove or with Sauté on Low, adding 2 tablespoons broth per cup, until the shrimp and rice reach 165°F. Freezing is not recommended because shrimp toughen and the rice loses its creamy texture.
notes: Do not substitute long-grain rice; Arborio's starch and absorption are central to the method.
For a mild family dinner, omit chile threads from the shared pot and offer crushed red pepper only at the table.
Total time includes roughly 10 minutes to pressurize, the controlled release and the shrimp-finishing stage.
Written for a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Check the minimum-liquid, fill-limit and venting directions for your exact model.
Rice expands and can foam, so stay below the half-full line and never place a towel over the release valve.

faqs.q: Why isn't the risotto creamy when I open the lid?
faqs.a: Pressure-cooked rice often looks loose and separate at first. Stir firmly for 30 to 60 seconds to release surface starch, then add butter and cheese; it will tighten further during the two-minute rest.
Yes, but thaw them completely in the refrigerator, drain and pat dry before seasoning. Ice and excess water would dilute the risotto and make the shrimp cook unevenly.

faqs.q: Can I make the risotto ahead?
faqs.a: It is best immediately after cooking. If necessary, pressure-cook the rice, release pressure and hold it for no more than 10 minutes before using Sauté to cook the shrimp and finish the dish.

title: South African-Style Lamb Bobotie with Raisin Rice & Chutney
dek: Gently curried lamb, fruit and almonds bake beneath a golden egg custard and arrive with turmeric-raisin rice and tangy chutney.
image_alt: Golden custard-topped lamb bobotie with bay leaves in a terracotta dish beside turmeric raisin rice and dark fruit chutney
ingredients: 2 slices firm white sandwich bread, crusts removed
1 1/2 cups basmati rice, rinsed and drained
1/2 tsp ground turmeric, for the rice
1/3 cup golden raisins, for the rice
1/2 cup mango or apricot chutney, for serving

instructions.name: Soak the bread
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 350°F. Tear the bread into a bowl, add 1 cup milk and soak for 10 minutes. Squeeze the bread gently over the bowl, reserving the milk, then mash the softened bread with a fork.

instructions.name: Brown the lamb
instructions.text: Heat the oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium. Cook the onion for 6 minutes. Add the lamb and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, breaking it into small pieces, until no pink remains and it reaches 160°F. Drain excess fat if more than 2 tablespoons collect.

instructions.name: Build the spiced filling
instructions.text: Stir in garlic, curry powder, coriander, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric, cinnamon, 1 teaspoon salt and pepper for 30 seconds. Fold in the mashed bread, preserves, Worcestershire, vinegar, 1/3 cup raisins and half the almonds. Cook for 2 minutes, then spread in a lightly oiled 9-by-13-inch baking dish.

instructions.name: Add the custard
instructions.text: Measure the reserved soaking milk and add enough fresh milk to equal 1 1/4 cups. Whisk it with the eggs and remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt. Pour over the lamb, arrange the bay leaves on top and scatter with the remaining almonds.

instructions.name: Bake until safely set
instructions.text: Bake for 30 to 35 minutes, until the custard is golden, no liquid ripples at the center and an instant-read thermometer in the middle registers 160°F. Rest for 10 minutes before serving.

instructions.name: Cook the raisin rice
instructions.text: While the bobotie bakes, combine the rice, water, remaining 1/2 teaspoon turmeric and a pinch of salt in a saucepan. Bring to a boil, cover, reduce to low and cook for 15 minutes. Remove from heat, fold in the remaining 1/3 cup raisins, cover for 10 minutes, then fluff. Serve the bobotie with raisin rice and chutney.

why_it_works: Milk-soaked bread binds the lamb filling without making it dense, while fruit, vinegar and mild curry create the characteristic sweet-savory balance.
Browning the lamb to 160°F before baking develops flavor and removes excess fat so the egg topping sets cleanly.
The custard bakes into a distinct golden cap, and turmeric-raisin rice plus tangy chutney echo the colors and accompaniments in the licensed photograph.
swaps: Use lean ground beef instead of lamb, cooking it to 160°F; add 1 extra tablespoon oil if the pan becomes dry.
Replace almonds with toasted pumpkin seeds for a nut-free version and tell diners about the substitution.
Use gluten-free sandwich bread and certified gluten-free Worcestershire sauce for a gluten-free adaptation.
storage: Cool within 2 hours and refrigerate bobotie and rice in separate airtight containers for up to 4 days. Reheat covered at 325°F with a splash of milk until the bobotie reaches 165°F; microwave the rice with 1 tablespoon water per portion to 165°F. Freeze the baked bobotie without rice for up to 2 months.
notes: Choose a mild curry powder for the shared casserole and serve chile sauce separately for anyone who wants heat.
Do not skip the 10-minute rest; it lets the custard and meat filling settle into tidy portions.
Remove the bay leaves before eating; they are aromatic but not pleasant to chew.

faqs.q: Can I assemble bobotie ahead of time?
faqs.a: Prepare and refrigerate the cooked lamb filling one day ahead. Bring it toward room temperature for 20 minutes, add the freshly whisked custard and bake until the center reaches 160°F; it may need 5 extra minutes.

faqs.q: Why did the custard disappear into the meat?
faqs.a: The filling was likely too hot or loosely packed. Let the cooked lamb stand 5 minutes, press it evenly into the dish and pour the custard slowly over the back of a spoon.

faqs.q: Is bobotie supposed to taste very spicy?
faqs.a: This version is aromatic rather than hot. Mild curry, coriander, turmeric and cinnamon provide warmth; chutney and preserves soften the spices, while hot sauce stays optional at the table.

title: Jamaican Ackee & Saltfish with Lime Slaw and Tomatoes
dek: Flaky salt cod, tender canned ackee, sweet peppers and thyme make a savory breakfast platter with crisp lime slaw and juicy tomatoes.
image_alt: Jamaican ackee and saltfish with red and green peppers beside creamy cabbage-carrot slaw and tomato wedges on a yellow plate
ingredients: 1/2 small green cabbage, finely shredded, about 5 cups
1/3 cup plain Greek yogurt or mayonnaise
1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more only if needed
2 cans canned ackee in brine, 19 oz each, drained very gently
3 medium ripe tomatoes, cut into wedges
Scotch bonnet hot sauce, optional for serving

instructions.name: Desalt the cod
instructions.text: Cover the salt cod with cold water and refrigerate for 8 to 24 hours, changing the water two or three times. For a same-day method, cover with fresh water in a saucepan, simmer for 10 minutes, drain and repeat once. Taste a small flake; it should be pleasantly seasoned, not aggressively salty.

instructions.name: Cook and flake the fish
instructions.text: Cover the desalted cod with fresh water, bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, until opaque, flaky and 145°F. Drain, cool briefly, remove any skin or bones and break into large flakes.

instructions.name: Make the lime slaw
instructions.text: Toss the cabbage, carrot and half the scallions with yogurt, 1 tablespoon lime juice, the honey and 1/4 teaspoon salt. Refrigerate while the skillet cooks so the cabbage softens slightly but stays crisp.

instructions.name: Sauté the aromatics
instructions.text: Heat the oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium. Cook the onion and both peppers for 6 to 8 minutes, until softened but still colorful. Add garlic, thyme, allspice and black pepper and cook for 30 seconds.

instructions.name: Fold in saltfish and ackee
instructions.text: Add the flaked cod and remaining scallions and cook for 2 minutes. Add the drained ackee and 1 tablespoon lime juice. Fold with a wide spatula only two or three times so the tender lobes remain intact; cook 3 minutes, until steaming hot. Taste before adding any of the remaining salt.

instructions.name: Build the photographed platter
instructions.text: Divide the ackee and saltfish among plates. Add a mound of lime slaw and tomato wedges, then finish with lime zest. Keep the shared platter mild and offer Scotch bonnet sauce only at the table.

why_it_works: Repeated soaking and gentle simmering tame salt cod while preserving enough seasoning to flavor the mild ackee.
Ackee is folded in at the end with minimal stirring, keeping its soft yellow lobes distinct rather than turning them into a paste.
Cool lime slaw and fresh tomato balance the rich fish-and-ackee skillet and reproduce the colorful composed plate in the licensed image.
swaps: If boneless salt cod is unavailable, use bone-in salted cod and inspect every flake carefully after simmering.
Use mayonnaise for a richer slaw or Greek yogurt for more tang; both should stay cold until serving.
Orange or yellow sweet pepper can replace either bell pepper without changing the cooking time.
storage: Cool the ackee and saltfish within 2 hours and refrigerate separately from the slaw and tomatoes for up to 3 days. Reheat the fish mixture gently in a covered skillet until it reaches 165°F, folding as little as possible. Keep the slaw refrigerated and use within 2 days. Freezing the ackee mixture is not recommended because the lobes become mealy.
notes: Use commercially canned ackee from a reputable producer, drain it well and never substitute raw or unripe fresh ackee, which can be dangerous.
Salt cod varies greatly in salinity; tasting after desalting is more reliable than a fixed number of water changes.
The 60-minute total assumes the salt cod was soaked overnight; the repeated same-day simmer method adds about 25 minutes.
The photo shows distinct ackee lobes, fish flakes, peppers, slaw and tomato, so gentle handling and separate plating matter.

faqs.a: Commercial canned ackee is processed and ready to heat after draining. Handle it gently and warm it through in the finished skillet; do not use unripe or home-prepared fresh ackee.

faqs.q: Can I shorten the salt-cod soaking time?
faqs.a: Yes. Use the repeated simmer-and-drain method, then taste a cooled flake before continuing. If it remains very salty, simmer it once more in fresh water.

faqs.q: Why did my ackee turn mushy?
faqs.a: It was probably stirred too often or boiled. Drain without pressing, add it only after the vegetables and fish are ready, and fold with a broad spatula over medium heat.

title: Classic Passionfruit & Berry Pavlova with Whipped Cream
dek: A crisp ivory meringue shell with a marshmallow-soft center carries billowy cream, tart passionfruit and a generous crown of berries.
image_alt: Rustic round pavlova topped with whipped cream, strawberries, raspberries, blueberries and golden passionfruit pulp
ingredients: 6 large egg whites, 200 g, at room temperature

instructions.name: Prepare the oven and pan
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 300°F with a rack in the lower third. Trace a 9-inch circle on parchment, turn the marked side down and place it on a heavy sheet pan. Wipe a clean mixer bowl and whisk with vinegar to remove any grease.

instructions.name: Whip a stable meringue
instructions.text: Beat the egg whites, cream of tartar and salt on medium until foamy, then on medium-high to soft peaks. Add the superfine sugar 1 tablespoon at a time over 5 to 7 minutes. Beat until the meringue is thick, glossy and forms stiff peaks; rub a little between your fingers to confirm no obvious sugar grit remains.

instructions.name: Fold and shape
instructions.text: Sift the cornstarch over the meringue. Add the white wine vinegar and 1/2 teaspoon vanilla and fold gently just until incorporated. Mound inside the traced circle, shaping a tall round with a shallow well in the center and rustic swirls around the edge.

instructions.name: Bake low and slow
instructions.text: Put the pan in the oven and immediately reduce the temperature to 250°F. Bake for 90 minutes without opening the door. The shell should feel dry and look pale ivory; a few fine cracks are normal.

instructions.name: Cool gradually
instructions.text: Turn off the oven, prop the door open about 1 inch with a wooden spoon and leave the pavlova inside for 90 minutes. Transfer it on the parchment to a rack and cool completely. This slow temperature change limits large cracks and collapse.

instructions.name: Top immediately before serving
instructions.text: Beat the cold cream, confectioners' sugar and remaining 1/2 teaspoon vanilla to medium peaks. Slide the pavlova onto a platter, spoon cream into the center, arrange the strawberries, raspberries and blueberries over it, then spoon on the passionfruit pulp and seeds. Slice with a serrated knife and serve within 30 minutes.

why_it_works: Gradual sugar addition creates a smooth, stable foam that dries into a crisp shell while retaining a marshmallow-soft center.
Cornstarch and vinegar help the center stay tender, while the long low bake and slow oven cooling reduce weeping and dramatic cracks.
Tart passionfruit and berries cut through sweet meringue and rich cream, matching every prominent topping visible in the licensed photograph.
swaps: Use blackberries or sliced kiwi in place of one berry, keeping the total fruit close to 20 ounces so the shell is not overloaded.
Pasteurized carton egg whites can work only if the package specifically says they are suitable for whipping; weigh 200 grams and expect a longer whipping time.
For a dairy-free topping, use the firm cream from chilled full-fat coconut milk and add it just before serving.
storage: Store the completely cooled, untopped shell airtight at cool room temperature for up to 24 hours. Refrigerate assembled leftovers loosely covered for up to 1 day; the shell will soften but remains safe to eat. Do not freeze an assembled pavlova. Refrigerate whipped cream and cut fruit promptly and discard after 2 hours at room temperature.
notes: Separate eggs while cold, then bring the whites to room temperature; even a trace of yolk or grease can prevent full volume.
If superfine sugar is unavailable, pulse granulated sugar briefly in a food processor without turning it into powder.
Humidity softens meringue, so bake on the driest day available and keep the cooled shell airtight until topping.

faqs.a: Small cracks are expected. Large splits usually come from undissolved sugar, overbeating, a hot oven or rapid cooling. Add sugar slowly, verify a smooth foam and cool the shell gradually in the switched-off oven.

faqs.q: How far ahead can I make it?
faqs.a: Bake the shell one day ahead and keep it airtight at room temperature. Whip the cream and prepare the fruit shortly before serving, then assemble within 30 minutes of slicing.

faqs.q: How do I know the meringue is baked?
faqs.a: After 90 minutes at 250°F, the outside should feel dry and release from the parchment at the edge while remaining pale. The center is intentionally soft, so do not keep baking until the entire shell is hard.
